content.title: How to Watch the Northern Lights for a Second Time This Week
content.text: Northern Lights. Credit : SERGEI GAPON/AFP via Getty NEED TO KNOW A coronal mass ejection from the sun could trigger northern lights visible in 16 U.S. states tonight, March 31The northern lights may extend farther south if geomagnetic storm activity strengthens beyond current predictionsSkywatchers should seek dark, elevated locations and prepare for peak activity tonight before it eases tomorrow Keep an eye on the night sky tonight, because the sun just fired something our way! A fast-moving cloud of charged solar particles, known as a coronal mass ejection (CME) per NASA, is currently barreling toward Earth — and if it grazes our planet as predicted, it could ignite a dazzling northern lights display tonight. ​​The northern lights (aurora borealis) result from geomagnetic storms, which occur when charged particles from the sun collide with gases in Earth's atmosphere, creating brilliant waves of light in the sky. Still, their visibility depends on several factors, including intensity and location. According to NOAA’s Space Weather Prediction Center, forecasters say geomagnetic activity is likely to intensify today as the CME approaches. The solar blast erupted during an X1.4-class solar flare on March 30, triggering strong radio blackouts, and is now racing through space. If you’re wondering what that means for skywatchers, it’s important to note that if geomagnetic storms strengthen, auroras can stretch far beyond their usual polar regions. If activity reaches G3 levels, for instance, the northern lights could dip unusually far south. Here’s everything you need to know about when, where and how to watch this stellar event. Related Stories When will the northern lights be visible? Aurora Borealis over ski slope in Levi. Alex Nicodim/Anadolu via Getty Head outside as soon as it gets dark enough! Geomagnetic activity is expected to ramp up before nightfall and linger overnight, but it is expected to peak at moderate (G2) storm levels tonight, March 31, and gradually ease to minor (G1) levels by Wednesday, April 1, according to NOAA’s latest forecast. Where will the northern lights be visible? Auroras in Beiji Village, Mohe Cit. Chi Shiyong/VCG via Getty Keep in mind that the northern lights can be fickle by nature, so be sure to keep tabs on the aurora forecast. According to NOAA, 16 U.S. states will appear fully or partially above the aurora view line, including Alaska, North Dakota, Minnesota, Montana, Wisconsin, South Dakota, Idaho, Michigan, Maine, Vermont, New Hampshire, Washington, Oregon, Iowa, New York and Wyoming. Still, if conditions strengthen when the CME hits, the northern lights could reach farther south than predicted. The same applies if conditions don’t align. How to watch the northern lights? Northern Lights. As always, you'll want to be prepared to witness this cosmic spectacle. Choose a location far away from city lights with a wide, unobstructed view of the northern horizon. Elevated spots with minimal light pollution offer the clearest views. You'll also want to wait at least 20 minutes for your eyes to adjust to the dark. How to photograph the northern lights? Auroras Borealis in Iceland. Getty Hoping to make some magical memories? Your smartphone is more than enough to do the trick! All you have to do is go to settings, turn on Night Mode and point your camera lens towards the sky.If you’re a more seasoned stargazer and happen to have a DSLR or mirrorless camera, grab a tripod and set your camera to manual mode. Remember, patience is key.
